[SCENE I]

Enter [the future] Edward the First, malcontented, with Lacy, Earl of Lincoln; John Warren, Earl of Sussex, and Ermsby, gentleman; Rafe Simnell, the King's fool.

Lacy.

1Why looks my lord like to a troubled sky
2When heaven's bright shine is shadowed with a fog?
3Alate we ran the deer and through the launds
4Stripped with our nags the lofty frolic bucks
5That scudded 'fore the teasers like the wind.
6Ne'er was the deer of merry Fressingfield
7So lustily pulled down by jolly mates,
8Nor shared the farmers such fat venison,
9So frankly dealt, this hundred years before;
10Nor have I seen my lord more frolic in the chase,
11And now changed to a melancholy dump.

Warren.

12After the Prince got to the keeper's lodge
13And had been jocund in the house awhile,
14Tossing of ale and milk in country cans,
15Whether it was the country's sweet content,
16Or else the bonny damsel filled us drink,
17That seemed so stately in her stammel red,
18Or that a qualm did cross his stomach then,
19But straight he fell into his passions.

Ermsby.

20Sirrah Rafe, what say you to your master?
21Shall he thus all amort live malcontent?

Rafe.

22Hearest thou, Ned?−Nay, look if he will speak 23to me.

Edward.

24What say'st thou to me, fool?

Rafe.

25I prithee tell me, Ned, art thou in love with the 26keeper's daughter?

Edward.

27How if I be, what then?

Rafe.

28Why then, sirrah, I'll teach thee how to deceive Love.

Edward.

29How, Rafe?

Rafe.

30Marry, sirrah Ned, thou shalt put on my cap and 31my coat and my dagger, and I will put on thy clothes and thy 32sword, and so thou shalt be my fool.

Edward.

33And what of this?

Rafe.

34Why, so thou shalt beguile Love, for Love is such a 35proud scab that he will never meddle with fools nor children. Is 36not Rafe's counsel good, Ned?

Edward.

37Tell me, Ned Lacy, didst thou mark the maid,
38How lively in her country weeds she looked?
39A bonnier wench all Suffolk cannot yield.
40All Suffolk? Nay, all England holds none such.

Rafe.

41Sirrah Will Ermsby, Ned is deceived.

Ermsby.

42Why, Rafe?

Rafe.

43He says all England hath no such, and I say, and
44I'll stand to it, there is one better in Warwickshire.

Warren.

45How provest thou that, Rafe?

Rafe.

46Why, is not the abbot a learned man, and hath read 47many books, and thinkest thou he hath not more learning than 48thou to choose a bonny wench? Yes, I warrant thee, by his whole 49grammar.

Ermsby.

50A good reason, Rafe.

Edward.

51I tell thee, Lacy, that her sparkling eyes
52Do lighten forth sweet Love's alluring fire,
53And in her tressesshe doth fold the looks
54Of such as gaze upon her golden hair;
55Her bashfull white mixed with the morning's red,
56Luna doth boast upon her lovely cheeks;
57Her front is Beauty's table, where she paints
58The glories of her gorgeous excellence;
59Her teeth are shelves of precious margarites,
60Richly enclosed with ruddy coral cliffs.
61Tush, Lacy, she is Beauty's overmatch,
62If thou survey'st her curious imagery.

Lacy.

63I grant, my lord, the damsel is as fair
64As simple Suffolk's homely towns can yield;
65But in the court be quainter dames than she,
66Whose faces are enriched with honour's taint,
67Whose beauties stand upon the stage of fame
68And vaunt their trophies in the courts of love.

Edward.

69Ah, Ned, but hadst thou watched her as myself,
70And seen the secret beauties of the maid,
71Their courtly coynesswere but foolery.

Ermsby.

72Why, how watched you her, my lord?

Edward.

73Whenas she swept like Venus through the house,
74And in her shape fast folded up my thoughts,
75Into the milkhouse went I with the maid,
76And there amongst the cream bowls she did shine
77As Pallas 'mongst her princely huswifery.
78She turned her smock over her lily arms
79And dived them into milk to run her cheese;
80But, whiter than the milk her crystal skin,
81Checked with lines of azure, made her blush
82That art or nature durst bring for compare.
83Ermsby, if thou hadst seen, as I did note it well,
84How Beauty played the huswife, how this girl,
85Like Lucrece, laid her fingers to the work,
86Thou wouldest with Tarquin hazard Rome and all
87To win the lovely maid of Fressingfield.

Rafe.

88Sirrah Ned, wouldst fain have her?

Edward.

89Ay, Rafe.

Rafe.

90Why, Ned, I have laid the plot in my head thou 91shalt have her already.

Edward.

92I’ll give thee a new coat an learn me that.

Rafe.

93Why, sirrah Ned, we'll ride to Oxford to Friar Bacon. Oh, 94he is a brave scholar, sirrah; they say he is a brave necromancer, 95that he can make women of devils, and he can juggle cats into 96costermongers.

Edward.

97And how then, Rafe?

Rafe.

98Marry, sirrah, thou shalt go to him, and because thy father 99Harry shall not miss thee, he shall turn me into thee; and 100I'll to the court, and I'll prince it out, and he shall make thee 101either a silken purse, full of gold, or else a fine wrought smock.

Edward.

102But how shall I have the maid?

Rafe.

103Marry, sirrah, if thou be'st a silken purse full of gold, 104then on Sundays she'll hang thee by her side, and you must not 105say a word. Now, sir, when she comes into a great press of people, 106for fear of the cutpurse on a suddenshe'llswap thee into her 107plackerd; then, sirrah, being there you may plead for yourself.

Ermsby.

108Excellent policy!

Edward.

109But how if I be a wrought smock?

Rafe.

110Then she'll put thee into her chest and lay thee into 111lavender, and upon some good day she'll put thee on, and at 112night when you go to bed, then being turned from a smock to a 113man, you may make up the match.

Lacy.

114Wonderfully wisely counselled, Rafe.

Edward.

115Rafe shall have a new coat.

Rafe.

116God thank you when I have it on my back, Ned.

Edward.

117Lacy, the fool hath laid a perfect plot,
118Forwhy our country Margaret is so coy
119And stands so much upon her honest points,
120That marriage or no market with the maid.
121Ermsby, it must be necromantic spells
122And charms of art that must enchain her love,
123Or else shall Edward never win the girl.
124Therefore, my wags, we'll horse us in the morn,
125And post to Oxford to this jolly friar.
126Baconshall by his magic do this deed.

Warren.

127Content, my lord. And that's a speedy way
128To wean these headstrong puppies from the teat.

Edward.

129I am unknown, not taken for the prince;
130They only deem us frolic courtiers
131That revel thus among our liege's game.
132Therefore I have devised a policy.
133Lacy, thou know'st next Friday is Saint James',
134And then the country flocks to Harleston fair.
135Then will the Keeper's daughter frolic there
136And overshine the troop of all the maids
137That come to see and to be seen that day.
138Haunt thee disguised among the country swains;
139Feign thou'rt a farmer's son, not far from thence;
140Espy her loves, and who she liketh best;
141Cote him, and court her to control the clown.
142Say that the courtier tirèd all in green,
143That helped her handsomely to run her cheese
144And filled her father's lodge with venison,
145Commends him and sends fairings to herself;
146Buy something worthy of her parentage,
147Not worth her beauty, for, Lacy, then the fair
148Affords no jewel fitting for the maid.
149And when thou talkest of me, note if she blush.
150Oh, then she loves! But if her cheeks wax pale,
151Disdain it is. Lacy, send how she fares,
152And spare no time nor cost to win her loves.

Lacy.

153I will, my lord, so execute this charge
154As if that Lacy were in love with her.

Edward.

155Send letters speedily to Oxford of the news.

Rafe.

156And, sirrah Lacy, buy me a thousand thousand millionof fine bells.

Lacy.

157What wilt thou do with them,Rafe?

Rafe.

158Marry, every time that Ned sighs for the Keeper's 159daughter I'll tie a bell about him, and so within three or four 160days I will send word to his father Harry that his son and my 161master Ned is become Love's morris dance.

Edward.

162Well, Lacy, look with care unto thy charge,
163And I will haste to Oxford to the friar,
164That he by art, and thou by secret gifts,
165Mayst make me lord of merry Fressingfield.

Lacy.

166God send Your Honour your heart's desire.

Exeunt.

[SCENE II]

Enter Friar Bacon, with Miles, his poor scholar, with books under his arm; with them Burden, Mason, Clement, three doctors.

Bacon.

167Miles, where are you?

Miles.

168Hic sum, doctissime et reverendissime doctor.

Bacon.

169Attulisti nos libros meos de Necromantia?

Miles.

170Ecce quam bonum et quam iocundum, habitares libros 171in unum!

Bacon.

172Now, masters of our academic state,
173That rule in Oxford, viceroys in your place,
174Whose heads contain maps of the liberal arts,
175Spending your time in depth of learnèd skill,
176Why flock you thus to Bacon's secret cell,
177A friar newly stalled in Brazennose?
178Say what's your mind, that I may make reply.

Burden.

179Bacon, we hear that long we have suspect,
180That thou art read in magic's mystery;
181In pyromancy to divine by flames;
182To tell, by hydromancy, ebbs and tides;
183By aeromancy to discover doubts,
184To plain out questions, as Apollo did.

Bacon.

185Well, Master Burden, what of all this?

Miles.

186Marry, sir, he doth but fulfill, by rehearsing of these 187names, the fable of the fox and the grapes: that which is above 188us pertains nothing to us.

Burden.

189I tell thee, Bacon, Oxford makes report−
190Nay, England, and the court of Henry says−
191Thou'rt making of a brazen head by art
192Which shall unfold strange doubts and aphorisms
193And read a lecture in philosophy;
194And, by the help of devils and ghastly fiends,
195Thou mean'st, ere many years or days be past,
196To compass England with a wall of brass.

Bacon.

197And what of this?

Miles.

198What of this, master? Why, he doth speak mystically, 199for he knows if your skill fail to make a brazen head, yet Mother 200Waters'strong ale will fit his turn to make him have a copper 201nose.

Clement.

202Bacon, we come not grieving at thy skill,
203But joying that our academy yields
204A man supposed the wonder of the world.
205For, if thy cunning work these miracles,
206England and Europe shall admire thy fame,
207And Oxford shall, in characters of brass
208And statues such as were built up in Rome,
209Eternize Friar Bacon for his art.

Mason.

210Then, gentle friar, tell us thy intent.

Bacon.

211Seeing you come as friends unto the friar,
212Resolve you, doctors, Bacon can by books
213Make storming Boreas thunder from his cave,
214And dim fair Luna to a dark eclipse.
215The great archruler, potentate of hell,
216Trembles when Bacon bids him or his fiends
217Bow to the force of his pentageron.
218What art can work, the frolic friar knows,
219And therefore will I turn my magic books,
220And strain out necromancy to the deep.
221I have contrived and framed a head of brass
222(I made Belcephon hammer out the stuff),
223And that by art shall read philosophy.
224And I will strengthen England by my skill,
225That, if ten Caesars lived and reigned in Rome,
226With all the legions Europe doth contain,
227They should not touch a grass of English ground.
228The work that Ninus reared at Babylon,
229The brazen walls framed by Semiramis,
230Carved out like to the portal of the sun,
231Shall not be such as rings the English strand
232From Dover to the marketplace of Rye.

Burden.

233Is this possible?

Miles.

234I'll bring ye two or three witnesses.

Burden.

235What be those?

Miles.

236Marry, sir, three or four as honest devils and good 237companions as any be in hell.

Mason.

238No doubt but magic may do much in this,
239For he that reads but mathematic rules
240Shall find conclusions that avail to work
241Wonders that pass the common sense of men.

Burden.

242But Bacon roves a bow beyond his reach,
243And tells of more than magic can perform,
244Thinking to get a fame by fooleries.
245Have I not passed as far in state of schools
246And read of many secrets? Yet to think
247That heads of brass can utter any voice,
248Or, more, to tell of deep philosophy−
249This is a fable Aesop had forgot.

Bacon.

250Burden, thou wrong'st me in detracting thus;
251Bacon loves not to stuff himself with lies.
252But tell me 'fore these doctors, if thou dare,
253Of certain questions I shall move to thee.

Burden.

254I will. Ask what thou can.

Miles.

255Marry, sir, he'll straight be on your pickpack to 256know whether the feminine or the masculine gender be most 257worthy.

Bacon.

258Were you not yesterday, Master Burden, at Henley- 259upon-the-Thames?

Burden.

260I was. What then?

Bacon.

261What book studied you there on all night?

Burden.

262I? None at all, I read not there a line.

Bacon.

263Then, doctors, Friar Bacon's art knows naught.

Clement.

264What say you to this, Master Burden? Doth he not 265touch you?

Burden.

266I pass not of his frivolous speeches.

Miles.

267Nay, Master Burden, my master, ere he hath done 268with you, will turn you from a doctor to a dunce, and shake you 269so small that he will leave no more learning in you than is in Balaam's 270ass.

Bacon.

271Masters, for that learned Burden's skill is deep,
272And sore he doubts of Bacon's cabbalism,
273I'll show you why he haunts to Henley oft:
274Not, doctors, for to taste the fragrant air,
275But there to spend the night in alchemy,
276To multiply with secret spells of art.
277Thus private steals he learning from us all.
278To prove my sayings true, I'll show you straight
279The book he keeps at Henley for himself.

Miles.

280Nay, now my master goes to conjuration, take heed!

Bacon.

281Masters, stand still. Fear not, I'll show you but his 282book.

Here he conjures.

283Per omnes deos infernales, Belcephon!

Enter a woman [the Hostess of the Bell ] with a shoulder of mutton on a spit, and a devil.

Miles.

284Oh, master, cease your conjuration or you spoil all, for 285here's a she-devil come with a shoulder of mutton on a spit. You 286have marred the devil's supper; but no doubt he thinks our college 287fare is slender, and so hath sent you his cook with a shoulder 288of mutton to make it exceed.

Hostess.

289Oh, where am I, or what's become of me?

Bacon.

290What art thou?

Hostess.

291Hostess at Henley, mistress of the Bell.

Bacon.

292How camest thou here?

Hostess.

293As I was in the kitchen 'mongst the maids,
294Spitting the meat against supper for my guests,
295A motion moved me to look forth of door.
296No sooner had I pried into the yard,
297But straight a whirlwind hoisted me from thence,
298And mounted me aloft unto the clouds.
299As in a trance, I thought nor fearèd naught,
300Nor know I where or whither I was ta'en,
301Nor where I am, nor what these persons be.

Bacon.

302No? Know you not Master Burden?

Hostess.

303Oh, yes, good sir, he is my daily guest. −
304What, Master Burden, 'twas but yesternight
305That you and I at Henley played at cards.

Burden.

306I know not what we did. A pox of all conjuring 307friars!

Clement.

308Now, jolly friar, tell us, is this the book
309That Burden is so careful to look on?

Bacon.

310It is.− But, Burden, tell me now,
311Thinkest thou that Bacon's necromantic skill,
312Cannot perform his head and wall of brass,
313When he can fetch thine hostess in such post?

Miles.

314I'll warrant you, master, if Master Burden could conjure 315as well as you, he would have his book every night from 316Henley to study on at Oxford.

Mason.

317Burden, what, are you mated by this frolic friar?−
318Look how he droops! His guilty conscience
319Drives him to bash and makes his hostess blush.

Bacon.

320Well, mistress, for I will not have you missed,
321You shall to Henley to cheer up your guests
322'Fore supper 'gin.−Burden, bid her adieu,
323Say farewell to your hostess 'fore she goes.
324[To the devil] Sirrah, away, and set her safe at home.

Hostess.

325Master Burden, when shall we see you at Henley?

Exeunt Hostess and the Devil.

Burden.

326The devil take thee and Henley too!

Miles.

327Master, shall I make a good motion?

Bacon.

328What's that?

Miles.

329Marry, sir, now that my hostess is gone to provide supper, 330conjure up another spirit, and send Doctor Burden flying 331after.

Bacon.

332Thus, rulers of our academic state,
333You have seen the friar frame his art by proof.
334And as the college callèd Brazennose
335Is under him and he the master there,
336So surely shall this head of brass be framed,
337And yield forth strange and uncouth aphorisms;
338And hell and Hecate shall fail the friar,
339But I will circle England round with brass.

Miles.

340So be it et nunc et semper, amen.

Exeunt omnes.

[SCENE III]

Enter Margaret, the fair maid of Fressingfield, with Thomas [, Richard] and Joan, and other clowns; Lacy, disguised in country apparel.

Thomas.

341By my troth, Margaret, here's a weather is able to 342make a man call his father whoreson. If this weather hold, we shall 343have hay good cheap, and butter and cheese at Harleston will 344bear no price.

Margaret.

345Thomas, maids when they come to see the fair,
346Count not to make a cope for dearth of hay.
347When we have turned our butter to the salt,
348And set our cheese safely upon the racks,
349Then let our fathers it as they please.
350We country sluts of merry Fressingfield
351Come to buy needless naughts to make us fine,
352And look that young men should be frank this day,
353And court us with such fairings as they can.
354Phoebus is blithe, and frolic looks from heaven
355As when he courted lovely Semele,
356Swearing the pedlars shall have empty packs,
357If that fair weather may make chapmen buy.

Lacy.

358But, lovely Peggy, Semele is dead,
359And therefore Phoebus from his palace pries,
360And, seeing such a sweet and seemly saint,
361Shows all his glories for to court yourself.

Margaret.

362This is a fairing, gentle sir, indeed,
363To soothe me up with such smooth flattery.
364But learn of me, your scoff's to broad before.−
365Well, Joan, our beauties must abide their jests;
366We serve the turn in jolly Fressingfield.

Joan.

367Margaret, a farmer's daughter for a farmer's son!
368I warrant you the meanest of us both
369Shall have a mate to lead us from the church.−
370But, Thomas, what's the news? What, in a dump?
371Give me your hand; we are near a pedlar's shop;
372Out with your purse; we must have fairings now.

Thomas.

373Faith, Joan, and shall. I'll bestow a fairing on you, and 374then we will to the tavern, and snap off a pint of wine or two.

All this while Lacy whispers [to] Margaret in the ear.

Margaret.

375Whence are you, sir? Of Suffolk, for your terms 376are finer than the common sort of men?

Lacy.

377Faith, lovely girl, I am of Beccles by,
378Your neighbour, not above six miles from hence,
379A farmer's son, that never was so quaint
380But that he could do courtesy to such dames.
381But trust me, Margaret, I am sent in charge
382From him that revelled in your father's house,
383And filled his lodge with cheer and venison,
384Tirèd in green.
385[Offering a purse] He sent you this rich ,
386His token, that he helped you run your cheese,
387And in the milkhouse chatted with yourself.

Margaret.

388To me? You forget .

Lacy.

389Women are often weak in memory.

Margaret.

390Oh, pardon, sir, I call to mind the man.
391'Twere little manners to refuse his gift,
392And yet I hope he sends it not for love;
393For we have little leisure to debate of that.

Joan.

394What, Margaret, blush not. Maids must have their 395loves.

Thomas.

396Nay, by the mass, she looks pale as if she were 397angry.

Richard.

398[to Lacy] Sirrah, are you of Beccles? I pray, how doth goodman 399Cob? My father bought a horse of him−I'll tell you, , 400'a were good to be a gentleman's jade, for of all things the foul 401hilding could not abide a dung-cart.

Margaret.

402[aside] How different is this farmer from the rest,aparte
403That erst as yet hath pleased my wand'ring sight!
404His words are witty, quickened with a smile,
405His courtesy gentle, smelling of the court;
406Facile and debonaire in all his deeds,
407Proportioned as was Paris, when, in grey,
408He courted in the vale by Troy.
409Great lords have come and pleaded for my love−
410Who but the keeper's lass of Fressingfield?−
411And yet methinks this farmer's jolly son
412Passeth the proudest that hath pleased mine eye.
413But, Peg, disclose not that thou art in love,
414And show as yet no sign of love to him
415Although thou well wouldst wish him for thy love.
416Keep that to thee till time doth serve thy turnheroic_couplet
417To show the grief wherein thy heart doth burn. −
418Come, Joan and Thomas, shall we to the fair?
419You, Beccles man, will not forsake us now?

Lacy.

420Not whilst I may have such quaint girls as you.

Margaret.

421Well, if you chance to come by Fressingfield,
422Make but a step into the Keeper's lodge,
423And such poor fare as woodmen can afford−
424Butter and cheese, cream, and fat venison−
425You shall have store, and welcome therewithal.

Lacy.

426Gramercies, Peggy. Look for me ere long.

Exeunt omnes.

[SCENE IV]

Enter Henry the Third; the Emperor; the King of Castile; Eleanor,his daughter; Jaques Vandermast, a German.

Henry.

427Great men of Europe, monarchs of the West,
428Ringed with the walls of old Oceanus,
429Whose lofty is like the battlements
430That compassed high-built Babel in with towers,
431Welcome, my lords, welcome, brave Western kings,
432To England's shore, whose promontory cliffs
433Shows Albion is another little world.
434Welcome, says English Henry to you all,
435Chiefly unto the lovely ,
436Who dared for Edward's sake cut through the seas,
437And venture as Agenor's damsel through the deep,
438To get the love of Henry's wanton son.

Castile.

439England's rich monarch, brave Plantagenet,
440The Pyren Mounts, swelling above the clouds,
441That ward the wealthy Castile in with walls,
442Could not detain the beauteous Eleanor.
443But, hearing of the fame of Edward's youth,
444She dared to brook Neptunus' haughty pride
445And bide the brunt of froward Aeolus.
446Then may fair England welcome her the more.

Eleanor.

447After that English Henry, by his lords,
448Had sent prince Edward's lovely counterfeit,
449A present to the Castile Eleanor,
450The comely portrait of so brave a man,
451The virtuous fame discoursèd of his deeds,
452Edward's courageous resolution
453Done at the Holy Land 'fore Damas' walls,
454Led both mine eye and thought in equal links
455To like so of the English monarch's son
456That I attempted perils for his sake.

Emperor.

457Where is the Prince, my lord?

Henry.

458He posted down, not long since, from the court,
459To Suffolk side, to merry Framlingham,
460To sport himself amongst my fallow deer.
461From thence, by packets sent to Hampton House,
462We hear the Prince is ridden with his lords
463To Oxford, in the academy there
464To hear dispute amongst the learnèd men.
465But we will send forth letters for my son
466To will him come from Oxford to the court.

Emperor.

467Nay, rather, Henry, let us, as we be,
468Ride for to visit Oxford with our train.
469Fain would I see your universities
470And what learned men your academy yields.
471From Hapsburg have I brought a learnèd clerk
472To hold dispute with English orators.
473This doctor, surnamed Jaques Vandermast,
474A German born, passed into Padua,
475To Florence, and to fair Bologna,
476To Paris, Rheims, and stately Orleans,
477And, talking there with men of art, put down
478The chiefest of them all in aphorisms,
479In magic, and the mathematic rules.Canción
480Now let us, Henry, try him in your schools.

Henry.

481He shall, my lord, this motion likes me well.
482We'll progress straight to Oxford with our trains,
483And see what men our academy brings.−
484And, wonder Vandermast, welcome to me.
485In Oxford shalt thou find a jolly friar
486Called Friar Bacon, England's only flower.
487Set him but nonplus in his magic spells,
488And make him yield in mathematic rules,
489And for thy glory I will bind thy brows
490Not with a poet's garland made of bays,
491But with a coronet of choicest gold.
492Whilst then we flit to Oxford with our troops,
493Let's in and banquet in our English court.

.

[SCENE V]

Enter Rafe Simnell in Edward's apparel, Edward [disguised as Rafe], Warren [and] Ermsby, disguised as the prince's followers].

Rafe.

494Where be these vagabond knaves, that they attend 495no better on their master?

Edward.

496If it please Your Honour, we are all ready at an inch.

Rafe.

497Sirrah Ned, I'll have no more post-horse to ride on. 498I'll have another fetch.

Ermsby.

499I pray you, how is that, my lord?

Rafe.

500Marry, sir, I'll send to the Isle of Ely for four or five 501dozen of geese, and I'll have them tied six and six together with 502whipcord. Now upon their backs will I have a fair field-bed 503with a canopy. And so, when it is my pleasure, I'll flee into what 504place I please. This will be easy.

Warren.

505Your Honour hath said well, but shall we to Brazennose
506College before we pull off our boots?

Ermsby.

507Warren, well motioned. We will to the friar
508Before we revel it within the town.−
509Rafe, see you keep your countenance like a prince.

Rafe.

510Wherefore have I such a company of cutting knaves 511to wait upon me, but to keep and defend my countenance against 512all mine enemies? Have you not good swords and bucklers?

Enter Bacon and Miles [not at first noticing Edward, Ermsby, Warren and ]

Ermsby.

513Stay, who comes here?

Warren.

514Some scholar; and we'll ask him where Friar Bacon 515is.

Bacon.

516Why, thou arrant dunce, shall I never make thee good 517scholar? Doth not all the town cry out and say "Friar Bacon's 518subsizar is the greatest blockhead in all Oxford"? Why, thou canst 519not speak one word of true Latin.

Miles.

520No, sir? Yes. What is this else: Ego sum tuus homo,"I am 521your man"? I warrant you, sir, as good Tully's phrase as any is in 522Oxford.

Bacon.

523Come on, sirrah, what part of speech is Ego?

Miles.

524Ego, that is "I"; marry, nomen substantivo.

Bacon.

525How prove you that?

Miles.

526Why, sir, let him prove himself an 'a will. "I" can be 527heard, felt and understood.

Bacon.

528Oh, gross dunce!

Here beat him.

Edward.

529Come, let us break off this dispute between these two.−
530Sirrah, where is Brazennose College?

Miles.

531Not far from Coppersmiths' Hall.

Edward.

532What, dost thou mock me?

Miles.

533Not I, sir, but what would you at Brazennose?

Ermsby.

534Marry, we would speak with Friar Bacon.

Miles.

535Whose men be you?

Ersmby.

536Marry, scholar, here's our master.

Rafe.

537Sirrah, I am the master of these good fellows. Mayst 538thou not know me to be a lord by my reparel?

Miles.

539Then here's good game for the hawk; for here's the 540master fool and a covey of coxcombs. One wise man, I think, 541would springe you all.

Edward.

542Gog's wounds! Warren, kill him.

[ uses his magic to charm them, so that they can't draw their swords]

Warren.

543Why, Ned, I think the devil be in my sheath! I 544cannot get out my dagger.

Ermsby.

545Nor I mine. 'Swounds, Ned, I think I am bewitched.

Miles.

546A company of scabs! The proudest of you all draw 547your weapon, if he can. 548[Aside] See how boldly I speak now my master is by.

Edward.

549I strive in vain; but if my sword be shut
550And conjured fast by magic in my sheath,
551Villain, here is my fist.

Strike him a box on the ear.

Miles.

552[to Bacon] Oh, I beseech you conjure his hands, too, that he may 553not lift his arms to his head, for he is light-fingered.

Rafe.

554Ned, strike him. I'll warrant thee, by mine honour.

Bacon.

555What means the English prince to wrong my man?

Edward.

556To whom speakest thou?

Bacon.

557To thee.

Edward.

558Who art thou?

Bacon.

559Could you not judge, when all your swords grew fast,
560That Friar Bacon was not far from hence?
561Edward, King Henry's son and Prince of Wales,
562Thy fool disguised cannot conceal thyself.
563I know both Ermsby and the Sussex Earl,
564Else Friar Bacon had but little skill.
565Thou comest in post from merry Fressingfield,
566Fast-fancied to the keeper's bonny lass,
567To crave some succour of the jolly friar;
568And Lacy, Earl of Lincoln, hast thou left
569To treat fair Margaret to allow thy loves.
570But friends are men, and love can baffle lords;
571The Earl both woos and courts her for himself.

Warren.

572Ned, this is strange! The friar knoweth all.

Ermsby.

573Apollo could not utter more than this.

Edward.

574I stand amazed to hear this jolly friar
575Tell even the very secrets of my thoughts.−
576But, learnèd Bacon, since thou knowest the cause
577Why I did post so fast from Fressingfield,
578Help, friar, at a pinch, that I may have
579The love of lovely Margaret to myself.
580And, as I am true Prince of Wales, I'll give
581Living and lands to strength thy college state.

Warren.

582Good Friar, help the Prince in this.

Rafe.

583Why, servant Ned, will not the friar do it? Were 584not my sword glued to my scabbard by conjuration, I would cut 585off his head and make him do it by force.

Miles.

586In faith, my lord, your manhood and your sword is all alike; 587they are so fast conjured that we shall never see them.

Ermsby.

588What, Doctor, in a dump? Tush, help the Prince,

Bacon.

590Crave not such actions greater dumps than these?
591I will, my lord, strain out my magic spells,
592For this day comes the Earl to Fressingfield,
593And 'fore that night shuts in the day with dark
594They'll be betrothed each to other fast.
595But come with me; we'll to my study straight,
596And in a glass prospective I will show
597What's done this day in merry Fressingfield.

Edward.

598Gramercies, Bacon. I will quite thy pain.

Bacon.

599But send your train, my lord, into the town.
600My scholar shall go bring them to their inn.

Edward.

602Warren, leave me; and Ermsby, take the fool.
603Let him be master, and go revel it
604Till I and Friar Bacon talk awhile.

Warren.

605We will, my lord.

Rafe.

606Faith, Ned, and I'll lord it out till thou comest. I'll be 607Prince of Wales over all the black pots in Oxford.

Exeunt.

[SCENE VI]

Bacon and Edward goes into the study.

Bacon.

608Now, frolic Edward, welcome to my cell.
609Here tempers Friar Bacon many toys,
610And holds this place his consistory court,
611Wherin the devils pleads homage to his words.
612Within this glass prospective thou shalt see
613This day what's done in merry Fressingfield,
614'Twixt lovely Peggy and the Lincoln Earl.

Edward.

615Friar, thou glad'st me. Now shall Edward try
616How Lacy meaneth to his sovereign lord.

Bacon.

617Stand there and look directly in the glass.

Enter Margaret and Friar Bungay [as if in the magic . They are visible to Edward but cannot be heard by him]

618What sees my lord?

Edward.

619I see the keeper's lovely lass appear,
620As brightsome as the paramour of Mars,
621Only attended by a jolly friar.

Bacon.

622Sit still and keep the crystal in your eye.

Margaret.

623But tell me, Friar Bungay, is it true
624That this fair courteous country swain,

627Peggy, 'tis true.'Tis Lacy, for my life−

629Left by Prince Edward to procure his loves;

Margaret.

632Be what he will, his lure is but for lust.
633But did Lord Lacy like poor Margaret,

635Friar, I would his humble handmaid be,
636And, for great wealth, quite him with courtesy.

Bungay.

637Why, Margaret, dost thou love him?

Margaret.

638His personage, like the pride of vaunting Troy,
639Might well avouch to shadow Helen's scape;
640His wit is quick and ready in conceit,

642Courteous, ah, friar, full of pleasing smiles.
643Trust me, I love too much to tell thee more,
644Suffice to me he is England's paramour.

Bungay.

645Hath not each eye that viewed thy pleasing face

Margaret.

647Yes, Bungay, and would God the lovely earl
648Had that in esse that so many sought!

Bungay.

649Fear not; the friar will not be behind

Edward.

651I think the friar courts the bonny wench.
652Bacon, methinks he is a lusty churl.

Bacon.

653Now look, my lord.

Enter Lacy [disguised in country garb, as before]

Edward.

654Gog's wounds, Bacon, here comes Lacy!

Bacon.

655Sit still, my lord, and mark the comedy.

Bungay.

656Here's Lacy. Margaret, step aside awhile.

[They overhear Lacy's soliloquy]

Lacy.

657Daphne, the damsel that caught Phoebus fast
658And locked him in the brightness of her looks,
659Was not so beauteous in Apollo's eyes
660As is fair Margaret to the Lincoln Earl.
661Recant thee, Lacy! Thou art put in trust.
662Edward, thy sovereign's son, hath chosen thee,
663A secret friend, to court her for himself,
664And darest thou wrong thy prince with treachery?
665Lacy, love makes no exception of a friend,
666Nor deems it of a prince but as a man.
667Honour bids thee control him in his lust;
668His wooing is not for to wed the girl,
669But to entrap her and beguile the lass.
670Lacy, thou lovest; then brook not such abuse,
671But wed her, and abide thy prince's frown;
672For better die than see her live disgraced.

Margaret.

673Come, friar, I will shake him from his dumps.
674How cheer you, sir? A penny for your thought.
675You're early up; pray God it be the near.
676What, come from Beccles in a morn so soon?

Lacy.

677Thus watchful are such men as live in love,
678Whose eyes brook broken slumbers for their sleep.
679I tell thee, Peggy, since last Harleston fair
680My mind hath felt a heap of passions.

Margaret.

681A trusty man, that court it for your friend!
682Woo you still for the courtier all in green?
683I marvel that he sues not for himself.

Lacy.

684Peggy, I pleaded first to get your grace for him,
685But when mine eyes surveyed your beauteous looks,
686Love, like a wag, straight dived into my heart,
687And there did shrine the idea of yourself.
688Pity me, though I be a farmer's son,
689And measure not my riches, but my love.

Margaret.

690You are very hasty, for to garden well
691Seeds must have time to sprout before they spring.
692Love ought to creep as doth the dial's shade,
693For timely ripe is rotten too too soon.

Bungay.

694Deus hic! Room for a merry friar.
695What, youth of Beccles, with the keeper's lass?
696'Tis well. But, tell me, hear you any news?

Margaret.

697No, friar. What news?

Bungay.

698Hear you not how the pursuivants do post
699With proclamations through each country town?

Lacy.

700For what, gentle friar? Tell the news.

Bungay.

701Dwell'st thou in Beccles and hear'st not of these news?
702Lacy, the Earl of Lincoln, is late fled
703From Windsor court, disguisèd like a swain,
704And lurks about the country here unknown.
705Henry suspects him of some treachery,
706And therefore doth proclaim in every way
707That who can take the Lincoln Earl shall have,

Lacy.

709The Earl of Lincoln! Friar, thou art mad,
710It was some other, thou mistakest the man.
711The Earl of Lincoln! Why, it cannot be.

Margaret.

712Yes, very well, my lord, for you are he;
713The Keeper's daughter took you prisoner.
714Lord Lacy, yield. I'll be your jailer once.

Edward.

715How familiar they be, Bacon!

Bacon.

716Sit still and mark the sequel of their loves.

Lacy.

717Then am I double prisoner to thyself.
718Peggy, I yield. But are these news in jest?

Margaret.

719In jest with you, but earnest unto me,
720Forwhy these wrongs do wring me at the heart.
721Ah, how these earls and noble men of birth
722Flatter and feign to forge poor women's ill!

Lacy.

723Believe me, lass, I am the Lincoln Earl,
724I not deny; but tirèd thus in rags

Margaret.

726What love is there where wedding ends not love?

Lacy.

727I meant, fair girl, to make thee Lacy's wife.

Margaret.

728I little think that earls will stoop so low.

Lacy.

729Say, shall I make thee countess ere I sleep?

Margaret.

730Handmaid unto the Earl, so please himself.
731A wife in name, but servant in obedience.

Lacy.

732The Lincoln Countess, for it shall be so!
733I'll plight the bands and seal it with a kiss.

Edward.

734Gog's wounds, Bacon, they kiss! I'll stab them!

Bacon.

735Oh, hold your hands, my lord, it is the glass!

Edward.

736Choler to see the traitors 'gree so well,
737Made me think the shadows substances.

Bacon.

738'Twere a long poniard, my lord, to reach between
739Oxford and Fressingfield, but sit still and see more.

Bungay.

740Well, Lord of Lincoln, if your loves be knit,
741And that your tongues and thoughts do both agree,
742To avoid ensuing jars, I'll hamper up the match.
743I'll take my portace forth and wed you here;
744Then go to bed and seal up your desires.

Lacy.

745Friar, content!−Peggy, how like you this?

Margaret.

746What likes my lord is pleasing unto me.

Bungay.

747Then handfast hand, and I will to my book.

Bacon.

748What sees my lord now?

Edward.

749Bacon, I see the lovers hand in hand,
750The friar ready with his portace there
751To wed them both. Then am I quite undone.
752Bacon, help now, if e'er thy magic served,
753Help, Bacon. Stop the marriage now,
754If devils or necromancy may suffice,
755And I will give thee fourty thousand crowns.

Bacon.

756Fear not, my lord, I'll stop the jolly friar
757For mumbling up his orisons this day.

[Bacon puts a spell on Bungay]

Lacy.

758Why speak'st not, Bungay? Friar, to thy book.

Bungay is mute, crying "Hud, hud".

Margaret.

759How lookest thou, friar, as a man distraught!
760Reft of thy senses, Bungay? Show by signs,
761If thou be dumb, what passions holdeth thee.

Lacy.

762He's dumb indeed. Bacon hath with his devils
763Enchanted him, or else some strange disease
764Or apoplexy hath possessed his lungs.
765But Peggy, what he cannot with his book
766We'll 'twixt us both unite it up in heart.

Margaret.

767Else let me die, my lord, a miscreant.

Edward.

768Why stands Friar Bungay so amazed?

Bacon.

769I have struck him dumb, my lord; and if Your Honour please,
770I'll fetch this Bungay straightway from Fressingfield,
771And he shall dine with us in Oxford here.

Edward.

772Bacon, do that, and thou contentest me.

Lacy.

773Of courtesy, Margaret, let us lead the friar
774Unto thy father's lodge, to comfort him
775With broths to bring him from this hapless trance.

Margaret.

776Or else, my lord, we were passing unkind
777To leave the friar so in his distress.

Enter a devil, and carry Bungay on his back [and so ]

778O, help, my lord! A devil, a devil, my lord!
779Look how he carries Bungay on his back!
780Let's hence, for Bacon's spirits be abroad.

Exeunt [Margaret and ]

Edward.

781Bacon, I laugh to see the jolly friar
782Mounted upon the devil, and how the Earl
783Flees with his bonny lass for fear!
784As soon as Bungay is at Brazennose,
785And I have chatted with the merry friar,
786I will in post hie me to Fressingfield
787And quite these wrongs on Lacy ere it be long.

Bacon.

788So be it, my lord. But let us to our dinner;
789For ere we have taken our repast awhile
790We shall have Bungay brought to Brazennose.

[SCENE VII]

Enter three doctors: Burden, Mason, [and] Clement.

Mason.

791Now that we are gathered in the Regent House,
792It fits us talk about the King's repair;
793For he, trooped with all the Western kings
794That lie alongst the Danzig seas by east,
795North by the clime of frosty Germany,
796The Almain monarch, and the Saxon duke,
797Castile, and lovely Eleanor with him,
798Have in their jests resolved for Oxford town.

Burden.

799We must lay plots of stately tragedies,
800Strange comic shows, such as proud Roscius
801Vaunted before the Roman emperors,
802To welcome all the western potentates.

Clement.

803But more, the King by letters hath foretold
804That Frederick, the Almain emperor,
805Hath brought with him a German of esteem,
806Whose surname is Don Jaques Vandermast,
807Skilful in magic and those secret arts.

Mason.

808Then must we all make suit unto the friar,
809To Friar Bacon that he vouch this task,
810And undertake to countervail in skill
811The German; else there's none in Oxford can
812Match and dispute with learnèd Vandermast.

Burden.

813Bacon, if he will hold the German play,
814We'll teach him what an English friar can do.
815The devil, I think, dare not dispute with him.

Clement.

816Indeed, Mas' Doctor, he pleasured you,
817In that he brought your hostess with her spit
818From Henley posting unto Brazennose.

Burden.

819A vengeance on the friar for his pains!
820But, leaving that, let's hie to Bacon straight
821To see if he will take this task in hand.

Clement.

822Stay, what rumour is this? The town is up in a mutiny.
823What hurly-burly is this?

Enter a Constable, with Rafe [disguised as Prince Edward], Warren, Ermsby and Miles.

Constable.

824Nay, masters, if you were ne'er so good, you shall 825before the doctors to answer your misdemeanour.

Burden.

826What's the matter, fellow?

Constable.

827Marry, sir, here's a company of rufflers that, drinking 828in the tavern, have made a great brawl and almost killed 829the vintner.

Miles.

830Salve, Doctor Burden! This lubberly lurdane,romance_heroico
831Ill-shaped and ill-faced, disdained and disgraced,
832What he tells unto vobis, mentitur de nobis.

833Who is the master and chief of this crew?

Miles.

834Ecce asinum mundi, figura rotundi,romance_heroico
835Neat, sheat and fine, as brisk as a cup of wine.

836What are you?

Rafe.

837I am, Father Doctor, as a man would say, the bell-wether 838of this company. These are my lords, and I the Prince of Wales.

839Are you Edward, the King's son?

Rafe.

840Sirrah Miles, bring hither the tapster that drew the 841wine, and I warrant when they see how soundly I have broke his 842head, they'll say 'twas done by no less man than a prince.

844And why so, sir?

845For they say the Prince is a brave and a wise gentleman.

846Why, and thinkest thou, Doctor, that he is not so?

Ermsby.

849Whose face, shining with many a sugared smile,

851And yet, Master Doctor, to speak like a proctor,skeltonic

857Doctors, whose doting nightcaps are not capable of 858my ingenious dignity, know that I am Edward Plantagenet, 859whom if you displease will make a ship that shall hold all your 860colleges, and so carry away the Niniversity with a fair wind to 861the Bankside in Southwark. How say'st thou, Ned Warren, 862shall I not do it?

867And I, my lord, will have pioneers to undermine the 868town, that the very gardens and orchards be carried away for 869your summer walks.

876Why, hare-brained courtiers, are you drunk or mad,

885No, no! Out with your blades, and hamper these jades.skeltonic
886Have a flirt and a crash, now play revel-dash,

Mason.

889To the prison with them, constable!blank_verse

Warren.

890Well, doctors, seeing I have sported me
891With laughing at these mad and merry wags,
892Know that Prince Edward is at Brazennose,
893And this, attirèd like the Prince of Wales,
894Is Rafe, King Henry's only lovèd fool;
895I, Earl of Sussex; and this Ermsby,

899My lord, pardon us, we knew not what you were,

902I will, Master Doctor, and satisfy the vintner for his 903hurt; only I must desire you to imagine him all this forenoon the 904Prince of Wales.

905I will, sir.

[SCENE VIII]

Enter Prince Edward with his poniard in his hand, Lacy and Margaret.

Edward.

909Lacy, thou canst not shroud thy trait'rous thoughts,
910Nor cover as did Cassius all his wiles,
911For Edward hath an eye that looks as far
912As Lynceus from the shores of Grecia.
913Did not I sit in Oxford by the friar
914And see thee court the maid of Fressingfield,
915Sealing thy flattering fancies with a kiss?
916Did not proud Bungay draw his portace forth,
917And, joining hand in hand, had married you,
918If Friar Bacon had not struck him dumb,
919And mounted him upon a spirit's back,
920That we might chat at Oxford with the friar?
921Traitor, what answer'st? Is not all this true?

Lacy.

922Truth all, my lord, and thus I make reply.
923At Harlestone Fair, there courting for Your Grace,
924Whenas mine eye surveyed her curious shape,
925And drew the beauteous glory of her looks
926To dive into the centre of my heart,
927Love taught me that Your Honour did but jest,
928That princes were in fancy but as men;
929How that the lovely maid of Fressingfield
930Was fitter to be Lacy's wedded wife
931Than concubine unto the Prince of Wales.

Edward.

932Injurious Lacy! Did I love thee more
933Than Alexander his Hephestion?
934Did I unfold the passion of my love,
935And lock them in the closet of thy thoughts?
936Wert thou to Edward second to himself,
937Sole friend, and partner of his secret loves?
938And could a glance of fading beauty break
939The enchainèd fetters of such private friends?
940Base coward, false, and too effeminate
941To be corrival with a prince in thoughts!
942From Oxford have I posted since I dined,
943To quite a traitor 'fore that Edward sleep.

Margaret.

944'Twas I, my Lord, not Lacy, stepped awry;
945For oft he sued and courted for yourself,
946And still wooed for the courtier all in green.
947But I, whom fancy made but overfond,
948Pleaded myself with looks as if I loved;
949I fed mine eye with gazing on his face,
950And, still bewitched, loved Lacy with my looks.
951My heart with sighs, mine eyes pleaded with tears,
952My face held pity and content at once,
953And more I could not cipher out by signs
954But that I loved Lord Lacy with my heart.
955Then, worthy Edward, measure with thy mind
956If women's favours will not force men fall,
957If beauty and if darts of piercing love
958Is not of force to bury thoughts of friends.

Edward.

959I tell thee, Peggy, I will have thy loves.
960Edward or none shall conquer Margaret.
961In frigates bottomed with rich Shittim planks,
962Topped with the lofty firs of Lebanon,
963Stemmed and encased with burnished ivory
964And overlaid with plates of Persian wealth.
965Like Thetis shalt thou wanton on the waves
966And draw the dolphins to thy lovely eyes
967To dance lavoltas in the purple streams.
968Sirens, with harps and silver psalteries,
969Shall wait with music at thy frigate's stem
970And entertain fair Margaret with their lays.
971England and England's wealth shall wait on thee,
972Britain shall bend unto her prince's love
973And do due homage to thine excellence,
974If thou wilt be but Edward's Margaret.

Margaret.

975Pardon, my lord. If Jove's great royalty
976Sent me such presents as to Danaë,
977If Phoebus, tirèd in Latona's webs,
978Came courting from the beauty of his lodge,
979The dulcet tunes of frolic Mercury,
980Nor all the wealth heaven's treasury affords,

Edward.

982I have learned at Oxford, then, this point of schools:
983Ablata causa, tollitur effectus.
984Lacy, the cause that Margaret cannot love
985Nor fix her liking on the English prince,
986Take him away, and then the effects will fail.

Lacy.

989[Kneeling] Rather than live and miss fair Margaret's love,
990Prince Edward, stop not at the fatal doom,
991But stab it home; end both my loves and life.

Margaret.

992Brave Prince of Wales, honoured for royal deeds,
993'Twere sin to stain fair Venus' courts with blood.
994Love's conquests ends, my Lord, in courtesy.
995Spare Lacy, gentle Edward; let me die,

Edward.

997Lacy shall die as traitor to his lord.

Lacy.

998I have deserved it. Edward, act it well.

Margaret.

999What hopes the Prince to gain by Lacy's death?

Edward.

1000To end the loves 'twixt him and Margaret.

Margaret.

1001Why, thinks king Henry's son that Margaret's love
1002Hangs in the uncertain balance of proud Time,
1003That death shall make a discord of our thoughts?
1004No! Stab the Earl, and 'fore the morning sun
1005Shall vaunt him thrice over the lofty east,
1006Margaret will meet her Lacy in the heavens.

Lacy.

1007If aught betides to lovely Margaret
1008That wrongs or wrings her honour from content,
1009Europe's rich wealth nor England's monarchy
1010Should not allure Lacy to overlive.
1011Then, Edward, short my life and end her loves.

Margaret.

1012Rid me, and keep a friend worth many loves.

Lacy.

1013Nay, Edward, keep a love worth many friends.

Margaret.

1014And if thy mind be such as fame hath blazed,
1015Then, princely Edward, let us both abide
1016The fatal resolution of thy rage.
1017Banish thou fancy and embrace revenge,
1018And in one tomb knit both our carcasses,

Edward.

1020Edward, art thou that famous Prince of Walesaparte
1021Who at Damasco beat the Saracens,
1022And brought'st home triumph on thy lance's point,
1023And shall thy plumes be pulled by Venus down?
1024Is it princely to dissever lovers' leagues,
1025To part such friends as glory in their loves?
1026Leave, Ned, and make a virtue of this fault,
1027And further Peg and Lacy in their loves.
1028So in subduing fancy's passion,
1029Conquering thyself thou get'st the richest spoil. −
1030Lacy, rise up! Fair Peggy, here's my hand,
1031The Prince of Wales hath conquered all his thoughts,
1032And all his loves he yields unto the Earl.
1033Lacy, enjoy the maid of Fressingfield,

1037Humbly I take her of my sovereign,
1038As if that Edward gave me England's right,

1040And doth the English prince mean true?
1041Will he vouchsafe to cease his former loves,

Edward.

1044I will, fair Peggy, as I am true lord.

Margaret.

1045Then, lordly sir, whose conquest is as great
1046In conquering love as Caesar's victories,
1047Margaret, as mild and humble in her thoughts

1049Yields thanks, and, next Lord Lacy, doth enshrine

Edward.

1051Gramercy, Peggy. Now that vowes are passed,
1052And that your loves are not be revolt,
1053Once, Lacy, friends again, come, we will post
1054To Oxford; for this day the King is there
1055And brings for Edward Castile Eleanor.
1056Peggy, I must go see and view my wife;
1057I pray God I like her as I loved thee.

Margaret.

1061As it please Lord Lacy; but love's foolish looks
1062Think footsteps miles and minutes to be hours.

Lacy.

1063I'll hasten, Peggy, to make short return.−
1064But, please Your Honour, go unto the lodge.
1065We shall have butter, cheese, and venison.
1066And yesterday I brought for Margaret
1067A lusty bottle of neat claret wine.

Edward.

1069'Tis cheer, Lord Lacy, for an emperor,
1070If he respect the person and the place.
1071Come, let us in, for I will all this night

[SCENE IX]

Enter Henry, Emperor, Castile, [the Duke attendants of Saxony], Eleanor, Vandermast, Bungay[and other lords and attendants].

Emperor.

1073Trust me, Plantagenet, these Oxford schools
1074Are richly seated near the riverside,
1075The mountains full of fat and fallow deer,

1081That lordly are the buildings of the town,

1096Let it be this: whether the spirits of pyromancy

1097or geomancy be most predominant in magic.

1098I say, of pyromancy.heroic_couplet

1099And I, of geomancy.

Vandermast.

1100The cabbalists that write of magic spells,blank_verse
1101As Hermes, Melchie and Pythagoras,
1102Affirm that 'mongst the quadruplicity
1103Of elemental essence, terra is but thought
1104To be a punctum squarèd to the rest;
1105And that the compass of ascending elements
1106Exceed in bigness as they do in height,
1107Judging the concave circle of the sun
1108To hold the rest in his circumference.
1109If, then, as Hermes says, the fire be great'st,
1110Purest, and only giveth shapes to spirits,
1111Then must these demons that haunt that place
1112Be every way superior to the rest.

Bungay.

1113I reason not of elemental shapes,
1114Nor tell I of the concave latitudes,
1115Noting their essence nor their quality,
1116But of the spirits that pyromancy calls
1117And of the vigour of the geomantic fiends.
1118I tell thee, German, magic haunts the grounds,
1119And those strange necromantic spells
1120That work such shows and wondering in the world
1121Are acted by those geomantic spirits
1122That Hermes calleth terræ filii.
1123The fiery spirits are but transparent shades,
1124That lightly pass as heralds to bear news;
1125But earthly fiends, closed in the lowest deep,
1126Dissever mountains if they be but charged,
1127Being more gross and massy in their power.

Vandermast.

1128Rather, these earthly geomantic spirits
1129Are dull and like the place where they remain;
1130For, when proud Lucifer fell from the heavens,
1131The spirits and angels that did sin with him
1132Retained their local essence as their faults,
1133All subject under Luna's continent.
1134They which offended less hang in the fire,
1135And second faults did rest within the air;
1136But Lucifer and his proud-hearted fiends
1137Were thrown into the centre of the earth,
1138Having less understanding than the rest,
1139As having greater sin and lesser grace.
1140Therefore such gross and earthly spirits do serve
1141For jugglers, witches and vile sorcerers,
1142Whereas the pyromantic genii
1143Are mighty, swift, and of far-reaching power.
1144But, grant that geomancy hath most force,
1145Bungay, to please these mighty potentates,

Bungay.

1147I will.

1148Now, English Harry, here begins the game;

1150What wilt thou do?

Vandermast.

1155Well done.

1156What say you, royal lordings, to my friar?

1164Hercules Prodi, Prodi, Hercules!

1165Quis me vult?

1166Jove's bastard son, thou Libyan Hercules,

Hercules.

1169Fiat.

Vandermast.

1170Now, Bungay, if thou canst by magic charm,

Bungay.

1174I cannot.

Vandermast.

1175Cease, Hercules, until I give thee charge-
1176Mighty commander of this English isle,
1177Henry, come from the stout Plantagenets,
1178Bungay is learned enough to be a friar,
1179But to compare with Jaques Vandermast
1180Oxford and Cambridge must go seek their cells

Bacon.

1188All hail to this royal company,

1190Bungay, how stand'st thou as a man amazed!

1192What art thou that questions thus?

1193Men call me Bacon.

1198Bestir thee, Jaques, take not now the foil,

Vandermast.

1200Bacon, wilt thou dispute?

1203Raised Hercules to ruinate that tree

1205Set Hercules to work.

1208I dare not. See'st thou not great Bacon here,

1210By all the thrones and dominations,

1213Bacon, that bridles headstrong Belcephon,

1216How now, Vandermast, have you met with your match?

1217Never before was't known to Vandermast

1219Bacon doth more than art, or else I fail.

1220Why, Vandermast, art thou overcome?−
1221Bacon, dispute with him and try his skill.

1222I come not, monarchs, for to hold dispute
1223With such a novice as is Vandermast;
1224I come to have your royalties to dine
1225With Friar Bacon here in Brazennose.

Emperor.

1234Why, Bacon, whither dost thou send him?

Bacon.

1235To Hapsburg; there Your Highness, at return,

1237Bacon, thou hast honoured England with thy skill,

1239I will be English Henry to thyself.

Bacon.

1241With me, my lord. And, while I fit my cheer,
1242See where Prince Edward comes to welcome you,

1247Ned, where hast thou been?

1263Martial Plantagenet, Henry's high-minded son,

1370Peggy, the lovely flower of all towns,

"The blooms of the almond tree grow in a night, and vanish 1460in a morn; the flies hemerae, fair Peggy, take life with 1461the sun and die with the dew; fancy, that slippeth in with a 1462gaze, goeth out with a wink; and too timely loves have ever the 1463shortest length. Therefore 1466know, Margaret, I have chosen a Spanish lady to be my wife, 1467chief waiting-woman to the Princess Eleanor; a lady fair, 1468and no less fair than thyself, honourable and wealthy. Farewell. 1472Not thine nor his own, 1473Edward Lacy."

1952Dost thou know me?

1953Know you, sir? Why, are not you one of my master's 1954devils, that were wont to come to my master Doctor Bacon at 1955Brazennose?

Devil.

1956Yes, marry, am I.

Miles.

1957Good Lord, Master Plutus, I have seen you a thousand times at 1958my master's, and yet I had never the manners to make you drink. 1959But, sir, I am glad to see how conformable you are to the statute. 1960[To the audience] I warrant you he's as yeomanly a man as you shall 1961see. Mark you, masters, here's a plain honest man, without welt or guard 1962[To the devil] But I pray you, sir, do you come lately from hell?

Devil.

1963Ay, marry. How then?

Miles.

1964Faith, 'tis a place I have desired long to see. Have you not 1965good tippling houses there? May not a man have a lusty fire there, 1966a pot of good ale, a pair of cards, a swingeing piece of chalk, 1967and a brown toast that will clap a white waistcoat on a cup 1968of good drink?

Devil.

1969All this you may have there.

Miles.

1970You are for me, friend, and I am for you. But I pray 1971you, may I not have an office there?

Devil.

1972Yes, a thousand.What wouldst thou be?

Miles.

1973By my troth, sir, in a place where I may profit myself. 1974I know hell is a hot place, and men are marvellous dry, and 1975much drink is spent there. I would be a tapster.

Devil.

1976Thou shalt.

Miles.

1977There's nothing lets me from going with you but 1978that 'tis a long journey, and I have never a horse.

Devil.

1979Thou shalt ride on my back.

Miles.

1980Now surely here's a courteous devil, that for to pleasure his friend 1981will not stick to make a jade of himself. 1982[To the audience] But I pray 1983you, goodman friend, let me move a question to you.

Devil.

1984What's that?

Miles.

1985I pray you, whether is your pace a trot or an amble?

Devil.

1986An amble.

Miles.

1987'Tis well, but take heed it be not a trot.
1988But 'tis no matter, I'll prevent it.

Devil.

1989What dost?

Miles.

1990Marry, friend, I put on my spurs; for if I find your pace 1991either a trot or else uneasy, I'll put you to a false gallop. I'll make 1992you feel the benefit of my spurs.

Devil.

1993Get up upon my back.

Miles.

1994Oh, Lord, here's even a goodly marvel, when a man 1995rides to hell on the devil's back!

Exeunt roaring.

[SCENE XVI]

Enter the Emperor with a pointless sword, next the king of Castile, carrying a sword with a point; Lacy, carrying the globe; Edward; Warren, carrying a rod of gold with a dove on it; Ermsby with a crown and sceptre; Queen[Eleanor] with [Margaret] the fair maid of Fressingfield on her left hand; Henry; Bacon, with other lords attending.

Edward.

1996Great potentates, earth's miracles for state,
1997Think that Prince Edward humbles at your feet,
1998And for these favours, on his martial sword
1999He vows perpetual homage to yourselves,
2000Yielding these honours unto Eleanor.

Henry.

2001Gramercies, lordlings. Old Plantagenet,
2002That rules and sways the Albion diadem,
2003With tears discovers these conceivèd joys,
2004And vows requital, if his men-at-arms,
2005The wealth of England, or due honours done
2006To Eleanor, may quite his favourites.
2007But all this while, what say you to the dames,
2008That shine like to the crystal lamps of heaven?

Emperor.

2009If but a third were added to these two,
2010They did surpass those gorgeous images
2011That gloried Ida with rich beauty's wealth.

Margaret.

2012'Tis I, my lords, who humbly on my knee
2013Must yield her orisons to mighty Jove
2014For lifting up his handmaid to this state,
2015Brought from her homely cottage to the court,
2016And graced with kings, princes and emperors,
2017To whom (next to the noble Lincoln Earl)
2018I vow obedience and such humble love
2019As may a handmaid to such mighty men.

Eleanor.

2020Thou martial man that wears the Almain crown,
2021And you the Western potentates of might,
2022The Albion Princess, English Edward's wife,
2023Proud that the lovely star of Fressingfield,
2024Fair Margaret, countess to the Lincoln earl,
2025Attends on Eleanor−gramercies, lord, for her−
2026'Tis I give thanks for Margaret to you all,
2027And rest, for her, due bounden to yourselves.

Henry.

2028Seeing the marriage is solemnized,
2029Let's march in triumph to the royal feast−
2030But why stands Friar Bacon here so mute?

Bacon.

2031Repentant for the follies of my youth,
2032That magic's secret mysteries misled,
2033And joyful that this royal marriage
2034Portends such bliss unto this matchless realm.

Henry.

2035Why, Bacon,
2036What strange event shall happen to this land,
2037Or what shall grow from Edward and his queen?

Bacon.

2038I find by deep prescience of mine art,
2039Which once I tempered in my secret cell,
2040That here where Brute did build his Troynovant,
2041From forth the royal garden of a king
2042Shall flourish out so rich and fair a bud
2043Whose brightness shall deface proud Phoebus' flower,
2044And overshadow Albion with her leaves.
2045Till then Mars shall be master of the field,
2046But then the stormy threats of wars shall cease.
2047The horse shall stamp as careless of the pike,
2048Drums shall be turned to timbrels of delight.
2049With wealthy favours plenty shall enrich
2050The strand that gladded wand'ring Brut to see,
2051And peace from heaven shall harbour in these leaves
2052That gorgeous beautifies this matchless flower.
2053Apollo's hellitropian then shall stoop,
2054And Venus' hyacinth shall vail her top;
2055Juno shall shut her gilliflowers up,
2056And Pallas' bay shall bash her brightest green;
2057Ceres' carnation, in consort with those,Canción
2058Shall stoop and wonder at Diana's rose.

Henry.

2059This prophecy is mystical−
2060But, glorious commanders of Europa's love,
2061That makes fair England like that wealthy isle
2062Circled with Gihon and swift Euphrates
2063In royalizing Henry's Albion
2064With presence of your princely mightiness,
2065Let's march. The tables all are spread,
2066And viands such as England's wealth affordsCanción
2067Are ready set to furnish out the boards.
2068You shall have welcome, mighty potentates.
2069It rests to furnish up this royal feast.
2070Only your hearts be frolic, for the time
2071Craves that we taste of naught but jouissance.
2072Thus glories England over all the West.

Exeunt omnes.

  1. Nota del editorEditor's note First,

  3. Nota del editorEditor's note Rafe

    Rafe is a variant of Ralph, representing the traditional pronunciation of the name (Hanks, Harcastle and Hodges).     Pallas Athena, Zeus’s daughter, in ancient Greek mythology was the goddess of wisdom, craft and war. She was syncretised with the roman goddess Minerva.

  43. Nota del editorEditor's note Lucrece

    Lucrece was a virtuous Roman matron of a good family, raped by Sextus Tarquin, Tarquin the Proud’s son (534-510 a.C.), last king of Rome. To avoid the dishonour for the rape she killed herself by stabbing herself in the heart, an affair which triggered the end of the Roman monarchy. Shakespeare wrote The Rape of Lucrece about this story.

  185. Nota del editor digitalDigital editor's note old Oceanus,

    old Oceanus, the Atlantic Ocean. In the Greek mythology it was originally the name of a Titan, god of the river believed to encircle the earth, but later applied to the oceans, as opposed to the enclosed seas.

  186. Nota del editor digitalDigital editor's note Babel

    Babel, the high tower which appears in the Bible (Genesis 11), an origin myth meant to explain why the world’s peoples speak different languages. People agreed to build a city and a tower tall enough to reach heaven, and as a punishment God confounded their speech so that they can no longer understand each other.

  187. NotaNote

    Albion, earliest known name for the island of Britain. It was used by ancient Greek geographers from the 4th century BC and even earlier, who distinguished Albion from Ierne (Ireland) and from smaller members of the British Isles. The Greeks and Romans probably received the name from the Gauls or the Celts. The name Albion has been translated as “white land”; and the Romans explained it as referring to the chalk cliffs at dover (Latin albus, “white”).

  188. Nota del editor digitalDigital editor's note Agenor's damsel

    Agenor’s damsel, Europe, daughter of the Phoenician king Agenor of Tyre. Zeus assumed the shape of a bull and swam through the waves to Crete, carrying her off on his back.

Greene used the same joke in A Looking Glass, I. ii, 201: “it was a nose autem glorificam ...” etc. In addition, “popelare” is a pun with the word “popa” (which means “Pope”).

  637. Nota del editorEditor's note Cumentator

He was appointed dictator to save Rome in 217 BC after the defeat in the battle of Trasimeno against Hannibal.

  800. NotaNote

    Omne … dulci, taken from Horace (De Arte Poeticae, 343-344): “Omne tulit punctum qui miscuit utile dulci / Lectorem delectando, pariterque monendo”. The translation is “He wins universal applause who mingles the useful with the agreeable, at once delighting and instructing the reader”. It was a sort of motto for Robert Greene, since it appeared on the title-pages of Arbasto (1584), Penelopes Web (1587), Pandosto (1588), Perimedes (1588), in which Greene calls it his “old poesie”, and Ciceronis Amor (1589), and at the end of Friar Bacon (1594). The shorter form “Omne tulit punctum” was used for Menaphon (1589), Never Too Late (1590), James IV (1598) and Orpharion (1599).

L’onorevole historia di Fra Bacone e Fra Bungay

Robert Greene — EMOTHE0326_LonorevoleHistoriaDiFraBaconeEFraBungay

[ DRAMATIS PERSONAE.

  • Il Re Arrigo terzo
  • Eduardo, Principe di Galles, suo figliuolo
  • L’Imperatore di Germania
  • Il Re di Castiglia
  • Lacy, conte di Lincoln
  • Warren, conte di Sussex
  • Ermsby, gentiluomo
  • Ralph Simnel, buffone del Re
  • Fra Bacone
  • Miles, povero scolaro di Fra Bacone
  • Fra Bungay
  • Jaques Vandermast
  • Burden, }
  • Mason, }
  • Clemente, } Dottori di Oxford
  • Lamberto
  • Serlsby, } gentiluomini
  • Due scolari, loro figliuoli
  • Guardiano
  • Tomaso, }
  • Riccardo, } rustici
  • Birro
  • Un Corrierre
  • Signori, Rustici, ecc.
  • Eleonora, figliuola del Re di Castiglia
  • Margherita, figliuola del Guardiano, la Bella Fanciulla di Fressingfield
  • Giovanna, una ragazza del contado
  • L’Ostessa della Campana ad Henley
  • Un diavolo
  • Spirito in sembianza di Ercole ]

[SCENA I]

[Presso Fremingham.]

Entra il Principe Eduardo, triste in aspetto, con Lacy, Warren, Ermsby e Ralph Simnel.

Lacy.

1Perchè somiglia il mio signore a un cielo turbato,
2quando il lucido splendore del firmamento è ombrato da una nebbia?
3Pur ora abbiam cacciato il dàino, e per i prati
4raggiunto co’ nostri corsieri i maschi superbi e gai,
5che fuggivano innanzi ai veltri come il vento:
6mai non fu il dàino dell’allegra Fressingfield
7così gagliardamente abbattuto da giocondi compagni,
8nè divisero i fittaioli una così grassa selvaggina,
9tanto liberalmente distribuita, da cent’anni a questa parte;
10nè ho io mai veduto il mio signore più gaio nella caccia,
11ed ora in una melanconica mestizia.

Warren.

12Dopo che il principe venne alla capanna del Guardiano,
13e fu stato in letizia nella casa per un po’,
14tracannando birra e latte in rustici boccali,
15fosse la dolce contentezza della campagna,
16oppure la leggiadra damigella che ci versava da bere,
17che pareva così nobile nel suo rosso fustagno,
18o che una nausea gli traversasse lo stomaco allora,
19ma subito egli cadde nelle sue pene.

Ermsby.

20Messer Ralph, che dite voi al vostro padrone?
21Resterà egli così avvilito nella sua tristezza?

Ralph.

22Odi tu, Ned? — No, guarda se mi vuol parlare!

Principe Eduardo.

23Che dici tu a me, buffone?

Ralph.

24Ti prego, dimmi, Ned, sei tu innamorato della figliuola del Guardiano?

Principe Eduardo.

25E che dunque, se fossi?

Ralph.

26Ebbene, allora, messere, io t’insegnerò come ingannare Amore.

Principe Eduardo.

27Come, Ralph?

Ralph.

28Perdio, Messer Ned, tu indosserai il mio abito, e il mio berretto, e il mio pugnale, ed io i tuoi panni e la tua spada: e così tu sarai il mio buffone.

Principe Eduardo.

29E a che questo?

Ralph.

30Ebbene, così tu deluderai Amore; perchè Amore è una così superba scabbia, che mai non si mischierà a buffoni o bambini. Non è buono il consiglio di Ralph, Ned?

Principe Eduardo.

31Dimmi, Ned Lacy, hai tu notato la fanciulla,
32com’ella pareva amabile nelle sue rustiche vesti?
33Una più leggiadra ragazza non la dà tutto il Suffolk:
34Tutto il Suffolk! no, tutta l’Inghilterra non ne ha una simile.

Ralph.

35Messer Will Ermsby, Ned è in inganno.

Ermsby.

36Perchè, Ralph?

Ralph.

37Egli dice che tutta l’Inghilterra non ne ha una simile, ed io dico, e sostengo, che ce n’è una meglio nella contea di Warwick.

Warren.

38Come lo provi, Ralph?

Ralph.

39Ebbene, non è l’abate un dotto uomo, e che ha letto molti libri, e pensi tu ch’egli non abbia più dottrina di te per scegliere una leggiadra ragazza? sì, te lo garantisco, per tutta la sua grammatica.

Ermsby.

40Una buona ragione, Ralph.

Principe Eduardo.

41Io ti dico, Lacy, che i suoi occhi scintillanti
42balenan fuori il seducente fuoco del dolce amore;
43e nelle sue trecce ella avvolge gli sguardi
44di chi contempla la sua chioma d’oro;
45il proprio verecondo candore, misto al rosso del mattino,
46ostenta la Luna sulle sue amabili guance;
47la sua fronte è la tavola su cui la bellezza dipinge
48le glorie della sua magnifica eccellenza;
49i suoi denti sono banchi di preziose margherite,
50riccamente cinti da rupi di rubicondo corallo.
51Così, Lacy, ella è l’estremo della bellezza,
52se tu osservi le sue rare sembianze.

Lacy.

53Io riconosco, mio signore, che la damigella è assai bella,
54per quanto posson dare i modesti borghi del semplice Suffolk;
55ma nella corte ci son dame più aggraziate di lei,
56i cui volti sono ornati del colore dell’onore,
57le cui bellezze stan sulla scena della fama,
58e vantano i loro trofei nelle corti d’amore.

Principe Eduardo.

59Ah, Ned, ma se tu l’avessi guardata come me,
60e vedute le segrete bellezze della fanciulla,
61la loro cortigianesca ritrosia non ti parrebbe che scioccherìa.

Ermsby.

62Perchè, come la guardaste voi, mio signore?

Principe Eduardo.

63Quando ella incedeva come Venere per la casa,
64e nella sua figura avviluppava i miei pensieri,
65alla cascina io andai con la fanciulla,
66e là tra i vasi di panna ella splendeva
67come Pallade tra la sua principesca masserizia:
68ella rimboccò la sua camicia sulle sue braccia di giglio,
69e le tuffò nel latte per fare il suo cacio;
70ma, più bianca del latte, la sua pelle trasparente,
71screziata di linee azzurre, avrebbe fatto arrossire la donna
72che arte o natura avesse osato portare al paragone.
73Ermsby, se tu avessi veduto, com’io ho bene osservato,
74come la bellezza faceva da massaia, come questa fanciulla,
75simile a Lucrezia, poneva le sue dita al lavoro,
76tu, con Tarquinio, arrischieresti Roma e tutto
77per conquistare l’amabile fanciulla di Fressingfield.

Ralph.

78Messer Ned, ti piacerebbe d’averla?

Principe Eduardo.

79Sì, Ralph.

Ralph.

80Ebbene, Ned, io ho disposta la trama nella mia testa; tu l’avrai subito.

Principe Eduardo.

81Io ti darò un abito nuovo, se tu me l’insegni.

Ralph.

82Ebbene, messer Ned, noi cavalcheremo ad Oxford da fra Bacone: o, egli è un gran dotto, messere; dicono ch’egli sia un negromante, ch’egli possa far donne di diavoli, e mutar con prestigio gatti in fruttivendoli.

Principe Eduardo.

83E che poi, Ralph?

Ralph.

84Perdio, messere, tu andrai da lui; e perchè tuo padre Arrigo non senta la tua mancanza, egli trasformerà me in te; e io andrò alla Corte e farò in tutto il principe; ed egli farà di te o una borsa di seta piena d’oro o altrimenti una camicia finamente ricamata.

Principe Eduardo.

85Ma come avrò io la fanciulla?

Ralph.

86Perdio, messere, se tu sarai una borsa di seta piena d’oro, allora le domeniche ella t’attaccherà al suo fianco, e voi non dovete dire una parola. Ora, signore com’ella viene tra una grande folla di gente, per paura dei tagliaborse, di subito ti ficcherà nella tasca della sua gonnella; allora, messere, essendo là, voi potete dir da voi le vostre ragioni.

Ermsby.

87Eccellente accorgimento!

Principe Eduardo.

88Ma come farei, s’io fossi una camicia lavorata?

Ralph.

89Allora essa ti metterà nel suo forziere, ti porrà nello spigo, e un bel giorno ti indosserà.

Lacy.

90Consiglio maravigliosamente saggio, Ralph.

Principe Eduardo.

91Ralph avrà un abito nuovo.

Ralph.

92Iddio vi ringrazî quand’io l’ho sul mio dosso, Ned.

Principe Eduardo.

93Lacy, il buffone ha disposto una trama perfetta;
94perchè la nostra rustica Margherita è tanto ritrosa,
95ed è così ferma sul punto della sua onestà,
96che, fuor del matrimonio, non c’è nulla da fare con la fanciulla.
97Ermsby, voglion essere incanti negromantici,
98e fascini d’arte magica, che incatenino il suo amore,
99o altrimenti Eduardo mai non conquisterà la fanciulla.
100Pertanto, miei allegri compagni, noi monteremo a cavallo nella mattinata,
101e ci affretteremo ad Oxford da questo giocondo frate:
102Bacone con la sua magìa farà questa faccenda.

Warren.

103Sta bene, mio signore; e questa è una via spiccia
104per svezzare queste cùcciole testarde dalla mammella.

Principe Eduardo.

105Io sono sconosciuto non preso per il principe;
106essi ci credono soltanto gai cortegiani,
107che fan baldoria così alla caccia del loro sovrano:
108perciò io ho meditato uno stratagemma;
109Lacy, tu sai che venerdì prossimo è San Giacomo,
110e i campagnuoli affluiscono alla fiera di Harlston:
111allora la figlia del Guardiano si darà buon tempo colà,
112e splenderà su tutta la turba delle fanciulle,
113che vanno in quel giorno per vedere ed esser vedute.
114Mèscolati travestito tra quei villani,
115fingi d’esser figlio d’un fittavolo, di quelle parti,
116spia i suoi amori, e chi ella ami più;
117fatti innanzi, e fa a lei la corte, per tener a freno il bifolco;
118di’ che il cortigiano tutto vestito di verde,
119che l’aiutò garbatamente a fare il suo cacio,
120ed empì la capanna di suo padre di selvaggina,
121si raccomanda e la manda a salutare.
122Compra qualcosa di conveniente al suo parentado,
123non alla sua bellezza; perchè, Lacy, in questo caso alla fiera
124non troveresti un gioiello adatto alla fanciulla:
125e quando tu parli di me, osserva s’ella arrossisce:
126o, se sì, ella ama; ma se le sue guance impallidiscono,
127questo è disdegno. Lacy, mandami a dire com’ella si comporta,
128e non risparmiar tempo nè spesa per conquistare il suo amore.

Lacy.

129Mio signore, io eseguirò quest’incarico,
130come se Lacy fosse innamorato di lei.

Principe Eduardo.

131Manda subito notizie ad Oxford per lettere.

Ralph.

132E, Messer Lacy, comprami mille mille milioni di bei campanelli.

Lacy.

133E che vuoi farne, Ralph?

Ralph.

134Perdio, ogni volta che Ned sospira per la figlia del Guardiano, io gli appiccherò addosso un campanello: e così entro tre o quattro giorni manderò a dire a suo padre Arrigo, che il suo figliuolo, e mio padrone Ned, è diventato il moreschiere d’Amore.

Principe Eduardo.

135Bene, Lacy, prenditi cura dell’incarico avuto,
136ed io m’affretterò ad Oxford dal frate,
137ch’egli con la sua arte e tu con segreti doni
138mi possiate far signore dell’allegra Fressingfield.

Lacy.

139Iddio conceda a vostro onore il desiderio del suo cuore.

Exeunt.

[SCENA II.]

[La cella di Fra Bacone al Nasodibronzo.]

Entrano Fra Bacone, e Miles con libri sotto il braccio; Burden, Mason e Clemente.

Bacone.

140Miles, dove siete voi?

Miles.

141Hic sum, doctissime et revverendissime doctor.

Bacone.

142Attulisti nobis libros meos de necromantia?

Miles.

143Ecce quam bonum et quam jucundum habitare libros in unum!

Bacone.

144Ora, signori del nostro accademico stato,
145che governate in Oxford, vicerè nel vostro grado,
146le cui teste contengono le mappe delle arti liberali,
147e spendete il vostro tempo nelle profondità dell’erudita sapienza,
148perchè vi affollate voi così alla segreta cella di Bacone,
149un frate da poco installato nel Nasodibronzo?
150Dite qual’è il vostro animo, che io possa rispondere.

Burden.

151Bacone, noi udiamo ciò che da tempo abbiamo sospettato,
152che tu sei istruito ne’ misteri della magìa;
153in piromanzia, a indovinar dalle fiamme;
154a dire, per idromanzia, i flussi e i riflussi;
155per aeromanzia, a chiarire dubitazioni,
156a risolver problemi, come usava Apollo.

Bacone.

157Bene, Maestro Burden, e che per tutto ciò?

Miles.

158Perdio, signore, egli non fa che porre in atto, con ripetere questi nomi, la favola della volpe e dell’uva: ciò che è sopra di noi non ci concerne in nulla.

Burden.

159Io ti dico, Bacone, che per Oxford corre fama,
160anzi, tutta Inghilterra a la corte d’Arrigo dice
161che tu stai facendo per arte magica una testa di bronzo,
162che dichiarerà singolari dubbî e aforismi,
163e terrà una lettura di filosofia,
164e che, con l’aiuto di diavoli e di orrendi demonî,
165tu intendi, prima che molti anni o giorni sian passati,
166di cingere l’Inghilterra d’un muro di bronzo.

Bacone.

167E che per ciò?

Miles.

168Che per ciò, maestro! ebbene, egli parla alla guisa mistica; perchè egli sa che se la vostra maestrìa non riesce a fare una testa di bronzo, pure la birra forte di Mamma Waters compirà il suo ufficio di fargli avere un naso di rame.

Clemente.

169Bacone, noi non veniamo per dolerci della tua maestrìa,
170ma per rallegrarci che la nostra accademia produca
171un uomo ch’è ritenuto la maraviglia del mondo;
172perchè se la tua sapienza opererà questi miracoli,
173Inghilterra ed Europa ammireranno la tua fama,
174ed Oxford in caratteri di bronzo
175e in statue, come erano alzate in Roma,
176eternerà fra Bacone per la sua arte.

Mason.

177Dunque, nobile frate, dicci il tuo intento.

Bacone.

178Poichè voi venite come amici dal frate,
179convincetevi, dottori, che Bacone può co’ suoi libri
180fare tuonare il tempestoso Borea dalla sua spelonca,
181ed oscurare la vaga Luna con un’oscura eclissi.
182Il grande arcirettore, sovrano dell’inferno,
183trema quando Bacone ingiunge a lui o a’ suoi demonî
184di inchinarsi alla forza del suo pentagerone.
185Ciò che l’arte può operare, sa il gaio frate;
186e perciò io scartabellerò i miei libri magici,
187e spremerò la negromanzia fino al fondo.
188Io ho immaginata e foggiata una testa di bronzo,
189(ho fatto martellar la materia da Belcefonte),
190ed essa per arte leggerà filosofia.
191Ed io afforzerò l’Inghilterra con la mia maestria,
192così che se dieci Cesari vivessero e regnassero in Roma,
193con tutte le legioni che l’Europa contiene,
194essi non toccherebbero un filo d’erba della terra inglese;
195l’opera che Nino elevò in Babilonia,
196le mura di bronzo foggiate da Semiramide,
197intagliate come la porta del sole,
198non sarà pari a quella che circonderà le coste inglesi,
199da Dover alla piazza del mercato di Rye.

Burden.

200È ciò possibile?

Miles.

201Io vi porterò due o tre testimoni.

Burden.

202Quali?

Miles.

203Perdio, signore, tre o quattro dei più onesti diavoli e buoni compagnoni che siano in inferno.

Mason.

204Non v’è dubbio che in ciò la magìa possa far molto,
205perchè colui che studia solo le regole matematiche
206troverà conclusioni che valgono a operare
207maraviglie che superano il comune intendimento degli uomini.

Burden.

208Ma Bacone tira con l’arco oltre il suo segno,
209e parla di ciò che la magìa non può eseguire,
210pensando di farsi una fama con stravaganze.
211Non sono io andato innanzi come lui nelle scuole,
212e non ho letto di molti segreti? pure, pensare
213che teste di bronzo possano mandar fuori alcuna voce,
214o più, parlar di profonda filosofia,
215quest’ è una favola che Esopo aveva dimenticata.

Bacone.

216Burden, tu mi fai torto calunniandomi così.
217Bacone non ama rimpinzarsi di menzogne.
218Ma parlami innanzi a questi dottori, se tu osi,
219di certi problemi ch’io ti proporrò.

Burden.

220Va bene; chiedi ciò che puoi.

Miles.

221Perdio, signore, egli ti sarà subito addosso per sapere se è più degno il genere maschile o il femminile.

Bacone.

222Non foste voi ieri, Maestro Burden, ad Henley sul Tamigi?

Burden.

223Ci fui: e poi?

Bacone.

224Qual libro studiaste voi là tutta la notte?

Burden.

225Io! nessuno affatto; io non lessi colà una linea.

Bacone.

226Allora, dottori, l’arte di fra Bacone non sa nulla.

Clemente.

227Che dite voi di ciò, Maestro Burden? non vi tocca egli?

Burden.

228Io non mi curo de’ suoi frivoli discorsi.

Miles.
